overview: VACUUM is a Delta Lake maintenance command that physically deletes data files (Parquet) from storage that are no longer referenced by the current Delta transaction log and are older than a configurable retention threshold.

Delta Lake never deletes files in place during normal operations: UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, and OPTIMIZE write new files and mark old ones as removed in the transaction log, so stale files accumulate and cost storage until VACUUM cleans them up.

VACUUM is the cleanup half of the table lifecycle and directly trades off storage cost against time travel range: removing old files reclaims space but permanently destroys the ability to query or restore the table versions that depended on those files.
learningObjectives: Understand what files VACUUM removes, the role of the Delta transaction log, and the default 7-day (168-hour) retention window.
Learn how VACUUM interacts with and limits time travel, and how RETAIN n HOURS and DRY RUN control and preview its behavior.
Recognize the danger of lowering the retention period below the duration of concurrent reads and writes, which can corrupt in-flight queries.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: VACUUM is a Delta Lake operation that recursively scans a table's storage directory and permanently deletes data files that are no longer referenced by the latest version of the Delta transaction log AND whose modification timestamp is older than the retention threshold (default 7 days). It does not affect the transaction log files themselves within that window; it only garbage-collects orphaned and tombstoned data files.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of a Delta table like a document with full edit history. Every time you change data, Delta writes new files and keeps the old ones around so you can 'undo' (time travel) to a previous version. Over time these old files pile up and cost you money. VACUUM is the cleanup crew that throws out the old files you no longer need. By default it only throws out files older than 7 days, so your recent 'undo' history stays intact.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Delta Lake was open-sourced by Databricks in 2019 to bring ACID transactions to data lakes built on cloud object storage. Because object stores like S3 and ADLS have no native transactional delete, Delta adopted a copy-on-write model where old files are logically removed via the transaction log rather than physically deleted. VACUUM was introduced as the explicit garbage-collection mechanism, with a deliberately conservative 7-day default to protect long-running queries and time travel that early data lake users relied on.

whyItMatters.business: Stale data files silently inflate cloud storage bills. On large tables with frequent updates, un-vacuumed tombstoned files can multiply storage many times over, so regular VACUUM directly reduces cost while keeping a recent recovery window for auditing and rollback.
whyItMatters.engineering: VACUUM keeps the file count and storage footprint bounded, which prevents listing operations and metadata scans from degrading. It is a core part of table hygiene alongside OPTIMIZE, and engineers must reason carefully about retention to avoid breaking concurrent jobs.
whyItMatters.scalability: Without VACUUM, the number of physical files grows unbounded even though the logical table size stays constant. Bloated directories slow down file listing on object stores and increase the cost of every metadata operation, hurting scalability of the whole pipeline.
whyItMatters.cost: Object storage is billed per byte stored. Tombstoned files that no version references are pure waste; VACUUM is often the single biggest storage-cost lever on mutable Delta tables, sometimes reclaiming the majority of a table's physical footprint.
whyItMatters.reliability: Correctly configured retention guarantees that long-running reads and concurrent writes always find the files they expect. An overly aggressive VACUUM is one of the most common causes of FileNotFoundException failures in production, so getting it right is a reliability concern.

coreComponents.name: Delta Transaction Log (_delta_log)
coreComponents.definition: The ordered set of JSON and checkpoint files that record every add and remove of data files, defining which files belong to each table version.
coreComponents.purpose: Acts as the source of truth for which Parquet files are 'live'. VACUUM consults it to determine which files are still referenced by any retained version.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Tracks file additions (add actions) and logical removals (remove actions, or tombstones) with timestamps that VACUUM uses to decide eligibility.
coreComponents.examples: 00000000000000000005.json containing a 'remove' action with a deletionTimestamp for an old file replaced by an UPDATE.

coreComponents.name: Retention Threshold (RETAIN n HOURS)
coreComponents.definition: The minimum age a removed/orphaned file must reach before VACUUM is allowed to physically delete it; defaults to 168 hours (7 days).
coreComponents.purpose: Protects time travel history and in-flight queries by guaranteeing files remain on disk for at least this duration after being tombstoned.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Defines the boundary between 'safe to delete' and 'still needed'. Lowering it below concurrent operation duration is unsafe.
coreComponents.examples: VACUUM events RETAIN 168 HOURS keeps a week of history; RETAIN 0 HOURS deletes everything not in the current version (dangerous).

coreComponents.name: VACUUM Executor (DRY RUN vs apply)
coreComponents.definition: The Spark job that lists the table directory, diffs it against referenced files, applies the retention filter, and either reports (DRY RUN) or deletes the eligible files.
coreComponents.purpose: To safely reclaim storage. DRY RUN lets engineers preview exactly which files would be removed before committing to a destructive delete.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Recursively lists storage, computes the set of unreferenced files older than the threshold, and prints (DRY RUN) or removes them.
coreComponents.examples: VACUUM events DRY RUN lists candidate paths; VACUUM events actually deletes them.

internalWorking: VACUUM first reads the Delta transaction log to build the set of all data files referenced by the current table state (and, within the retention window, by recent versions still protected by tombstone timestamps).
It then recursively lists the physical table directory in object storage to enumerate every Parquet file actually present, including orphaned files from failed or uncommitted writes.

It computes the difference: files present on disk but not referenced by any protected version. From that candidate set it filters out any file whose modification time is newer than the retention threshold (now minus RETAIN n HOURS).

The remaining files are older than the threshold and unreferenced, so VACUUM deletes them from storage. The _delta_log files are not removed by VACUUM (log cleanup is governed separately by delta.logRetentionDuration, default 30 days).
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Transaction Log (referenced files) + Directory Listing (physical files) -> Diff (unreferenced files) -> Apply retention filter (older than RETAIN n HOURS) -> DRY RUN report OR physical delete from object storage
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A DELETE removes 1,000 rows from a Delta table; Delta writes new Parquet files for the surviving rows and adds 'remove' tombstones for the old files in a new log entry with a deletionTimestamp.
2. The old files remain physically on disk so time travel queries (SELECT ... VERSION AS OF) can still read the pre-delete state.
3. An engineer runs VACUUM mytable DRY RUN; the command reports the old files as candidates but only those older than 7 days.

4. After confirming, the engineer runs VACUUM mytable; files tombstoned more than 168 hours ago are physically deleted, storage is reclaimed, and time travel to those old versions now fails because the underlying files are gone.

keyTerminology.meaning: A 'remove' action recorded in the transaction log marking a data file as logically deleted from the table while it physically remains on disk.
keyTerminology.importance: VACUUM targets tombstoned (and orphaned) files; the tombstone's timestamp is what the retention threshold is measured against.

keyTerminology.meaning: The ability to query or restore a previous version of a Delta table using VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF.
keyTerminology.importance: VACUUM permanently limits time travel: once the files for an old version are deleted, that version becomes unqueryable.

keyTerminology.meaning: The minimum age (default 168 hours) a file must reach before VACUUM may delete it, set via RETAIN n HOURS.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the safety boundary that protects concurrent readers/writers and the recovery window; lowering it is dangerous.

keyTerminology.meaning: A data file present in storage that is not referenced by any table version, typically left by a failed or aborted write.
keyTerminology.importance: VACUUM cleans these up too, reclaiming space wasted by partial commits.

importantConcepts.explanation: Databricks blocks VACUUM with a retention shorter than 7 days by default, raising an error, because shorter windows risk deleting files still needed by concurrent operations. To override you must explicitly set spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled = false, which is a deliberate, dangerous opt-out.

VACUUM cleans data files; it does not clean the transaction log. Log files are retained per delta.logRetentionDuration (default 30 days). This means you might still see old log entries even after the corresponding data files have been vacuumed, but querying those versions will fail because the data is gone.

variationsAndTypes: **Default VACUUM:** VACUUM table_name with no clause uses the 7-day (168-hour) retention threshold.
**VACUUM ... RETAIN n HOURS:** Explicitly sets a custom retention window, e.g., RETAIN 720 HOURS for 30 days of history or a shorter window if the safety check is disabled.
**VACUUM ... DRY RUN:** Non-destructive preview that lists the files that would be deleted without actually removing them.
**Inventory-based VACUUM:** Newer Databricks runtimes support VACUUM ... USING INVENTORY to supply a pre-computed file listing, avoiding expensive recursive directory listing on huge tables.
advantages: **Storage Cost Reduction:** Reclaims object storage occupied by tombstoned and orphaned files, often the largest storage lever on mutable tables.
**Bounded File Count:** Prevents unbounded growth of physical files, keeping directory listings and metadata operations fast.
**Cleans Failed Writes:** Removes orphan files left behind by aborted or failed jobs, which are otherwise never reclaimed.
**Controllable Safety:** DRY RUN and the retention check provide guardrails so cleanup is predictable and reviewable before it destroys data.
disadvantages: **Destroys Time Travel History:** Vacuumed versions can no longer be queried or restored; this is irreversible.
**Risk to Concurrent Operations:** Aggressively low retention can delete files still being read by long-running queries, causing FileNotFoundException.
**Expensive Directory Listing:** On very large tables, the recursive listing step can be slow and costly without an inventory.
**No Log Cleanup:** It does not shrink the transaction log, so it only addresses one part of table growth.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Run VACUUM on mutable tables that accumulate tombstones (frequent MERGE/UPDATE/DELETE) or after OPTIMIZE, on a regular schedule, once you are confident no concurrent job or required time-travel window depends on the files being removed.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid lowering retention below the longest concurrent read/write duration, avoid VACUUM on tables where you need a long audit/recovery window unless retention is set accordingly, and avoid running it more aggressively than your time-travel SLA allows.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: VACUUM is like the recycling bin on your computer combined with a shredder on a timer. When you delete a file it goes to the bin (tombstone) and you can still recover it. VACUUM is the scheduled shredder that permanently destroys anything that has been in the bin for more than 7 days. If you set the timer too short, you might shred a file someone is still actively working on.

commonMisconceptions.myth: DELETE on a Delta table immediately frees up storage.
commonMisconceptions.reality: DELETE only writes new files and tombstones the old ones in the log; the physical files (and their storage cost) remain until VACUUM removes them after the retention period.

commonMisconceptions.myth: VACUUM with a low retention is fine as long as no one is querying right now.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A write or read started before VACUUM can still be reading older files mid-operation. Deleting those files out from under it causes failures, which is why the 7-day safety check exists.

productionConsiderations.scalability: On tables with millions of files, the recursive directory listing dominates VACUUM runtime. Use partition pruning where possible and consider USING INVENTORY or predictive optimization to avoid full listings.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Always keep retention at or above your longest concurrent operation and your time-travel SLA. Disabling retentionDurationCheck without this discipline is a leading cause of production FileNotFoundException incidents.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Because VACUUM cleans orphan files from failed writes, it improves storage hygiene after fault events; but it must run after those writes have either fully committed or fully aborted to avoid deleting in-progress files.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track the number of files and bytes deleted per VACUUM run, the runtime, and any FileNotFoundException errors in downstream jobs that correlate with a recent VACUUM as a signal that retention was too aggressive.
productionConsiderations.security: VACUUM permanently deletes data, so it must run with appropriate privileges. In regulated environments, a deliberately short retention plus VACUUM is also used to enforce data deletion (e.g., GDPR right-to-erasure) within the required window.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Schedule VACUUM regularly (e.g., daily or weekly) on high-churn tables to keep storage minimal, balancing the savings against the loss of time-travel range and the compute cost of the VACUUM job itself.
productionConsiderations.performance: Pair VACUUM with OPTIMIZE: OPTIMIZE compacts small files into large ones (creating many new tombstones), and a subsequent VACUUM reclaims the now-unreferenced small files, restoring both read performance and low storage cost.

codeExamples.title: Default VACUUM with DRY RUN preview
codeExamples.overview: Preview which files VACUUM would delete using the default 7-day retention, then apply it.
codeExamples.breakdown: DRY RUN lists candidate files without deleting them, letting you confirm scope. Running VACUUM without a RETAIN clause uses the default 168-hour threshold, deleting only unreferenced files older than 7 days.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: DRY RUN returns a list of file paths and a count/size summary; the applied VACUUM returns the path(s) cleaned and reclaims storage for files tombstoned more than 7 days ago.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting DRY RUN and running a destructive VACUUM directly; expecting it to delete recently deleted data (it will not, due to the 7-day window).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Always run DRY RUN first in production to verify the deletion set, and run VACUUM shortly after OPTIMIZE to reclaim the small files it replaced.

codeExamples.title: Custom retention and the safety override (dangerous)
codeExamples.overview: Setting a shorter retention requires explicitly disabling the safety check, which is risky.
codeExamples.breakdown: Databricks refuses a retention below 7 days unless retentionDurationCheck is disabled. The override exists for advanced cases (e.g., aggressive cost cleanup or compliance deletion) but removes the protection against deleting files used by concurrent operations.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The first statement raises an error. After disabling the check, VACUUM deletes files older than 24 hours; any concurrent long-running read/write older than 24 hours could now fail with FileNotFoundException.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Leaving the check disabled at the cluster/session level so all future VACUUMs are unsafe; running this while ETL jobs are mid-flight.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Only disable the check in an isolated maintenance window with no concurrent jobs, and re-enable it immediately after.

codeExamples.title: VACUUM with PySpark / DeltaTable API
codeExamples.overview: Programmatic VACUUM using the Delta Lake Python API, useful inside scheduled maintenance jobs.
codeExamples.code:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

delta_table = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "main.analytics.events")

# Vacuum with default 7-day retention (168 hours)
delta_table.vacuum()

# Vacuum with explicit retention of 720 hours (30 days)
delta_table.vacuum(retentionHours=720)

# Inspect history to see how time travel range is affected
delta_table.history().select("version", "timestamp", "operation").show(truncate=False)
codeExamples.breakdown: DeltaTable.forName loads the table handle. vacuum() with no argument uses the default retention; passing retentionHours sets a custom window. history() shows the available versions, helping you reason about what time travel remains after a VACUUM.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The vacuum() calls reclaim eligible files and return without error; history() shows the version log, but versions whose files were vacuumed will fail if you actually try to read them.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Passing a retentionHours value below 168 without disabling the check raises an exception; assuming history() rows guarantee the data is still readable.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Embed vacuum() in a scheduled maintenance notebook/job that also runs OPTIMIZE, and log the version/timestamp range before and after for auditability.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A clickstream events table receives constant MERGE upserts to deduplicate and correct late-arriving events. Over months, tombstoned files have ballooned storage to 5x the logical data size, inflating the cloud bill, while the team only needs 7 days of rollback capability.
endToEndExample.inputData: A partitioned Delta table main.analytics.events (partitioned by event_date) receiving hourly MERGE operations, each leaving behind tombstoned Parquet files from rewritten partitions.
endToEndExample.architecture: Delta Lake table on cloud object storage, governed by Unity Catalog, with a nightly maintenance Databricks Job that runs OPTIMIZE then VACUUM. Time-travel rollback SLA is 7 days; no batch job runs longer than 6 hours.
processingSteps: 1. Nightly maintenance job acquires no exclusive lock; it runs OPTIMIZE main.analytics.events to compact small files from the day's MERGEs.
2. The job runs VACUUM main.analytics.events DRY RUN and logs the candidate file count and total bytes.
3. It validates that retention (default 168 hours) comfortably exceeds the 6-hour max job duration and the 7-day rollback SLA.
4. It runs VACUUM main.analytics.events to physically delete files tombstoned more than 7 days ago, reclaiming storage.
5. It records pre- and post-VACUUM storage size and the available time-travel version range for auditing.
endToEndExample.output: Physical storage shrinks back toward the logical data size; the table retains exactly 7 days of time-travel history; downstream queries are unaffected because no operation runs longer than the retention window.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Dashboards track bytes/files deleted per night, table physical vs logical size ratio, VACUUM runtime, and any FileNotFoundException in downstream jobs.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If a downstream job reports FileNotFoundException after a VACUUM, the team treats it as a retention-too-low signal and increases the retention window; the maintenance job fails safe if OPTIMIZE has not completed.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Storage cost drops dramatically while preserving the required 7-day recovery window, and read performance stays high because OPTIMIZE plus VACUUM keeps the table compact and free of stale files.

industryUseCases.problem: High-velocity event tables with constant MERGE upserts accumulate enormous volumes of tombstoned files, multiplying storage cost.
industryUseCases.solution: Scheduled nightly VACUUM with the default 7-day retention following OPTIMIZE, reclaiming storage from rewritten partitions.
industryUseCases.benefits: Storage costs fall to near the logical data size while preserving a one-week rollback window for incident recovery.

industryUseCases.problem: Right-to-erasure (GDPR/CCPA) requires that deleted personal data be physically removed from storage within a defined SLA, not just logically deleted.
industryUseCases.solution: A controlled VACUUM with a retention set to the compliance window (e.g., RETAIN n HOURS) ensures DELETE'd records' underlying files are physically purged on schedule.
industryUseCases.benefits: Demonstrable compliance with data deletion mandates, with physical removal evidenced by the VACUUM audit log.

industryUseCases.problem: Nightly batch ETL that rewrites large dimension and fact tables leaves orphaned and tombstoned files that bloat the data lake.
industryUseCases.solution: VACUUM runs as part of the table-maintenance DAG, with DRY RUN gating in lower environments to validate scope before production deletion.
industryUseCases.benefits: Predictable, reviewable cleanup that keeps the lake compact and prevents directory-listing slowdowns on key tables.

productionDeepDive.scalability: VACUUM cost is dominated by listing every file under the table path. On petabyte tables with millions of files this is the bottleneck; using USING INVENTORY or letting predictive optimization manage it avoids full recursive listings. Partitioned tables benefit from listing being parallelized across partitions.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: VACUUM cleans orphan files left by failed writes, improving resilience, but it must only run when no write is mid-commit; otherwise it could delete files an in-progress transaction expects. Idempotent re-runs are safe because already-deleted files are simply skipped.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Because VACUUM is destructive, it is typically scheduled in maintenance windows. In always-on environments, keep retention well above the longest-running concurrent query so VACUUM can run anytime without disrupting readers.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Retention defines your recovery point for time-travel-based rollback. Set RETAIN to match your DR/rollback SLA; vacuuming below it eliminates the ability to RESTORE to those versions. Pair with regular RESTORE/CLONE backups for longer-horizon recovery.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Run VACUUM after OPTIMIZE so the small files OPTIMIZE replaces are reclaimed in the same cycle. Avoid over-frequent VACUUM on huge tables since the listing cost can exceed the storage savings; tune frequency to churn rate.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: VACUUM is usually the single biggest storage-cost reducer on mutable tables. Balance the storage savings against (a) the compute cost of the VACUUM job and (b) the value of the time-travel history you are destroying.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: VACUUM requires modify privileges on the table and permanently destroys data, so restrict who can run it and audit its execution. It also serves as the physical-deletion enforcement mechanism for compliance erasure requirements.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Capture VACUUM output (files/bytes removed), runtime, and correlate FileNotFoundException downstream errors with recent VACUUM runs. Track the physical-to-logical size ratio as a hygiene metric.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: VACUUM does not alter logical data, but verify after runs that the current table version still reads correctly and that any required time-travel versions remain accessible (i.e., were within retention).
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log every VACUUM with the retention used and the version range removed. Alert when retentionDurationCheck is disabled, when retention drops below the configured floor, or when a downstream FileNotFoundException follows a VACUUM.

recommendedPractices: **Always DRY RUN first in production** to review exactly which files will be deleted before committing.
**Keep retention >= longest concurrent operation and your time-travel SLA**; never lower it casually.
**Run VACUUM after OPTIMIZE** so the compacted-away small files are reclaimed in the same maintenance cycle.
**Schedule VACUUM regularly** (daily/weekly) on high-churn tables rather than running it reactively when storage spikes.
engineeringStandards: VACUUM must run as part of an automated, idempotent maintenance job, not ad-hoc on production tables.
Disabling spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck is forbidden outside isolated maintenance windows and must be re-enabled immediately.
Every VACUUM run must log the retention used and the version/timestamp range removed.
designRecommendations: Set table retention (and thus VACUUM behavior) to match the documented rollback/recovery SLA for that table.
For huge tables, adopt inventory-based VACUUM or predictive optimization to avoid expensive directory listings.
Separate maintenance compute from production read/write clusters to isolate the destructive operation.
namingConventions: Name maintenance jobs clearly, e.g., maint_optimize_vacuum_<table>, so destructive operations are easy to identify.
Tag VACUUM job runs with the table name and retention value in job parameters/metadata.
documentationStandards: Document each table's retention policy and its corresponding time-travel/rollback SLA.
Document any approved use of the retention safety override, including the justification and window.
Record the maintenance schedule (OPTIMIZE + VACUUM cadence) per table.
testingStrategies: In lower environments, validate VACUUM scope with DRY RUN against representative data before enabling in production.
Test that time travel to a version just inside the retention window still succeeds and just outside fails as expected.
Test concurrent-read safety by running a long query while VACUUM executes with proper retention to confirm no FileNotFoundException.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lowering retention below the duration of concurrent reads/writes (e.g., RETAIN 0 HOURS) to save storage.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers see large storage and want immediate reclamation, not realizing in-flight operations still reference recent files.
commonMistakes.impact: Concurrent or just-finished queries fail with FileNotFoundException because their data files were deleted out from under them.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Keep retention at or above the longest concurrent operation; only reduce it in an isolated maintenance window with no active jobs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting DELETE/UPDATE to immediately reclaim storage.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Assuming Delta deletes physically like a traditional database, when it actually tombstones files in the log.
commonMistakes.impact: Storage keeps growing despite logical deletes, and the team is surprised the bill does not drop until VACUUM runs.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Understand that physical reclamation only happens via VACUUM after the retention period; schedule VACUUM accordingly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running VACUUM with too-short retention and breaking time travel needed for an audit or rollback.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Treating VACUUM purely as a storage tool without accounting for the time-travel history it destroys.
commonMistakes.impact: Required RESTORE or VERSION AS OF queries fail permanently because the underlying files are gone and cannot be recovered.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Set retention to match the time-travel/recovery SLA; keep a longer window for tables that need auditing or rollback.

comparisonSection.explanation: VACUUM permanently deletes unreferenced files older than the retention period to reclaim storage and limit time travel. OPTIMIZE rewrites many small files into fewer large ones to improve read performance but adds storage (and tombstones) until VACUUM cleans up the replaced files. They are complementary: OPTIMIZE for speed, VACUUM for cost.

DELETE/UPDATE preserve old versions by tombstoning (you can still time travel). VACUUM is what actually destroys the files for old versions, permanently limiting how far back you can time travel. So mutations are reversible until VACUUM makes them irreversible.

DRY RUN is a non-destructive preview that lists candidate files and can be re-run freely. An applied VACUUM physically deletes files and is irreversible; there is no undo, so DRY RUN should gate any production VACUUM.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does the VACUUM command do in Delta Lake?
beginnerQuestions.answer: VACUUM physically deletes data files from storage that are no longer referenced by the current Delta table version and are older than the retention threshold (default 7 days), reclaiming storage occupied by tombstoned and orphaned files.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Stress that it removes physical files, not log entries, and only those past the retention window. Connect it to the fact that DELETE/UPDATE only tombstone files logically.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the default retention period for VACUUM and why is it 7 days?
beginnerQuestions.answer: The default is 7 days (168 hours). It is conservative to protect time travel history and, critically, to ensure files still being read by long-running concurrent queries are not deleted out from under them.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Highlight both reasons: protecting time travel and protecting in-flight operations. Mention the retentionDurationCheck guard.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does VACUUM interact with time travel?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Time travel relies on old data files remaining on disk. VACUUM permanently deletes files for versions older than the retention period, so any version whose files were vacuumed can no longer be queried with VERSION AS OF / TIMESTAMP AS OF or restored. VACUUM therefore sets the practical limit on how far back you can time travel.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Make clear the destruction is irreversible and that the transaction log may still list the version even though the data is gone.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why is it dangerous to set RETAIN to a very low value, and how do you even do it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: A low retention can delete files that concurrent or recently started reads/writes still need, causing FileNotFoundException. Databricks blocks retention below 7 days unless you set spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled = false, which is a deliberate, risky override that should only be used in an isolated maintenance window.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize the concurrency hazard and the explicit nature of the override; a good answer mentions re-enabling the check afterward.

advancedQuestions.question: Walk through exactly how VACUUM decides which files to delete.
advancedQuestions.answer: It reads the transaction log to build the set of files referenced by protected versions, recursively lists the physical table directory to find all files present, diffs the two to get unreferenced files, then filters out any whose modification time is newer than now minus the retention threshold. The remaining old, unreferenced files are deleted. The _delta_log itself is governed separately by logRetentionDuration.
advancedQuestions.explanation: A strong answer covers the log-vs-listing diff, the timestamp filter, orphan files from failed writes, and that VACUUM does not clean the log.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you use VACUUM to satisfy a GDPR right-to-erasure requirement?
advancedQuestions.answer: First DELETE the personal records (logical removal/tombstone), then run VACUUM with a retention set to the compliance window so the underlying files are physically purged within the required SLA. Because the default 7-day floor may exceed or meet the requirement, you set RETAIN accordingly and, if shorter than 7 days, carefully use the safety override in a controlled window, logging the run for audit.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests understanding that DELETE alone does not physically remove data and that VACUUM is the enforcement mechanism, plus awareness of the safety/audit implications.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your storage bill keeps rising even though the logical size of a frequently-MERGE'd table is flat. A junior engineer ran VACUUM table RETAIN 1 HOURS after disabling the safety check, and now a long-running downstream job is failing with FileNotFoundException. What happened and how do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Rising storage = tombstoned files never reclaimed. The fix for storage is VACUUM, but the junior engineer set retention (1 hour) below the downstream job's duration, so VACUUM deleted files the job was still reading. Need to restore safety and a sane retention.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: The 1-hour retention deleted files the long-running job still referenced, causing FileNotFoundException. Re-enable spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck, set retention back to at least the longest concurrent operation and the time-travel SLA (e.g., 168 hours), re-run the failed job from a clean state, and schedule VACUUM at the safe retention going forward.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a table maintenance strategy for a high-churn Delta table that must minimize storage cost while preserving a 7-day rollback window and never breaking concurrent batch jobs (max 4 hours).
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Run a nightly maintenance job: OPTIMIZE (and optionally ZORDER) to compact the day's MERGE output, then VACUUM DRY RUN to log scope, then VACUUM with default 168-hour retention. Keep retention at 168 hours, which exceeds both the 4-hour job duration and the 7-day rollback SLA.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Higher VACUUM frequency reclaims storage sooner but adds compute cost and risks listing overhead on large tables. Longer retention preserves more rollback history but keeps more storage. The chosen 7-day window balances cost, recovery, and concurrency safety.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: As the table grows to millions of files, switch to inventory-based VACUUM or enable predictive optimization so Databricks manages OPTIMIZE/VACUUM automatically, avoiding full recursive directory listings and tuning cadence to actual churn.

followUpQuestions: Does VACUUM remove the transaction log files? What controls log retention?
What happens to time travel for a version after its files have been vacuumed?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: VACUUM permanently deletes Delta data files no longer referenced by the table and older than the retention threshold (default 7 days), reclaiming storage at the cost of time travel.
keyConcepts: Tombstone: file logically removed in the log but still on disk.
RETAIN n HOURS: custom retention; below 7 days requires disabling the safety check.
DRY RUN: non-destructive preview of files to be deleted.
Destroys time travel for vacuumed versions; does NOT clean the _delta_log.
formulas: Deletable files = (files on disk) - (files referenced by protected versions), filtered to modificationTime < now - RETAIN hours
interviewPoints: DELETE/UPDATE only tombstone; VACUUM does physical deletion.
Default 7-day retention protects concurrent reads and time travel.
Lowering retention below concurrent operations causes FileNotFoundException.
Run VACUUM after OPTIMIZE to reclaim compacted-away small files.
VACUUM is irreversible; always DRY RUN first.
quickNotes: VACUUM does not touch the transaction log; delta.logRetentionDuration (default 30 days) governs that.
Time travel range is effectively bounded by your VACUUM retention.
retentionDurationCheck must be re-enabled after any temporary override.
Use inventory-based VACUUM / predictive optimization on very large tables to avoid costly listings.
VACUUM is the physical-deletion mechanism for GDPR/CCPA erasure compliance.

keyTakeaways: VACUUM permanently removes Delta data files that are no longer referenced and older than the retention threshold; DELETE/UPDATE/MERGE only tombstone files, so storage is reclaimed only when VACUUM runs.
The default retention is 7 days (168 hours), chosen to protect both time travel history and in-flight concurrent reads/writes.
VACUUM permanently limits time travel: once a version's files are vacuumed, that version can no longer be queried or restored.

Lowering retention below the duration of concurrent reads/writes (which requires disabling the retentionDurationCheck guard) risks FileNotFoundException failures and is one of the most dangerous Delta operations.
Use DRY RUN to preview deletions and run VACUUM after OPTIMIZE so the compacted-away small files are actually reclaimed.
